problem.title: Load Balancing gRPC & HTTP/2 Across Kubernetes Pods
problem.prompt: Your payment-ledger gRPC service runs on Kubernetes behind an AWS Network Load Balancer (L4). During a 10x traffic surge, HPA scales the backend from 4 to 24 pods, yet CPU stays at 98% on the original 4 pods while the 20 new pods sit at 3% CPU. Existing Java and Python gRPC clients keep sending 100% of their 45,000 RPS over their initial subchannels. Diagnose why L4 load balancing fails for HTTP/2 and design a zero-downtime fix.
requirements: Distribute gRPC RPCs evenly (<10% skew) across all 24 backend pods within 30 seconds of HPA scale-out.
Prevent connection storms or TLS handshake spikes when cycling long-lived HTTP/2 connections.
Support both Java (grpc-netty) and Python (grpcio) clients without dropping in-flight RPCs.
Maintain sub-15 ms p99 latency during pod scale-up and rolling deployments.
constraints: Peak aggregate throughput is 45,000 RPS across 120 client pods.
TLS 1.3 mTLS is mandatory on all service-to-service gRPC channels.
In-flight unary RPCs take up to 2 seconds and must complete gracefully before socket closure.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why did scaling from 4 to 24 pods leave the 20 new pods at 3% CPU while the original 4 stayed at 98%?

referenceMaterial.summary: L4 load balancers only route on TCP connection establishment (SYN). Because HTTP/2 multiplexes all gRPC calls onto one long-lived TCP subchannel per VIP, existing clients never open new connections to hit the 20 new pods.
approachSteps: Inspect active TCP connections (`ss -tnp | grep :9090`) on old vs. new pods.
Confirm `grpc_server_started_total` is 0 on newly scaled pods.
Identify that `ClusterIP` / NLB VIP returns 1 IP, causing `pick_first` to hold 1 TCP socket indefinitely.
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payment-ledger-headless
  namespace: prod
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: payment-ledger
  ports:
    - name: grpc
      port: 9090
      targetPort: 9090
tradeOffs: Headless DNS removes the L4 VIP bottleneck but requires clients to support round_robin LB.
Using an L7 Envoy proxy keeps a single VIP for external clients at the cost of +0.5 ms extra hop.
alternatives: Deploy Envoy or Linkerd/Istio L7 service mesh.
Use gRPC-xDS control plane for dynamic endpoint push.
failureModes: Leaving default `pick_first` policy on headless DNS still pins all traffic to the first returned IP.

stages.learnerPrompt: Design the client and server configuration changes for Java (`grpc-netty`) and Python (`grpcio`) to achieve <10% skew within 30s without dropping 2s in-flight RPCs.
Review the production Java server + client configuration with `round_robin`, `maxConnectionAge`, and `maxConnectionAgeGrace`.

referenceMaterial.summary: Combine headless DNS resolution with `round_robin` on the client and jittered `maxConnectionAge` + `maxConnectionAgeGrace` on the Netty server.
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
ManagedChannel channel = ManagedChannelBuilder
    .forTarget("dns:///payment-ledger-headless.prod.svc.cluster.local:9090")
    .defaultLoadBalancingPolicy("round_robin")
    .build();

Server server = NettyServerBuilder.forPort(9090)
    .maxConnectionAge(180, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .maxConnectionAgeGrace(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .addService(new LedgerServiceImpl())
    .build();
tradeOffs: 180s maxConnectionAge adds ~16 TLS handshakes/sec cluster-wide (negligible CPU).
Lower maxConnectionAge (e.g., 15s) speeds up rebalancing but increases TLS handshake CPU.
alternatives: Envoy L7 proxy with `lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST` for external clients.
failureModes: Omitting `maxConnectionAgeGrace` causes RST_STREAM on 2-second in-flight RPCs.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why choose headless DNS + `round_robin` over simply lowering `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` to 10 seconds behind the existing L4 NLB?

referenceMaterial.summary: Lowering `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` to 10s behind an L4 NLB still leaves each client with only 1 subchannel—meaning any single client's burst still hits 1 pod, and TLS 1.3 handshakes spike 18x.
approachSteps: Compare per-client fan-out: 1 subchannel behind VIP vs. 24 subchannels with headless DNS.
Calculate TLS 1.3 handshake rate: 2,880 / 10s = 288 handshakes/sec vs. 16 handshakes/sec.
Verify that `round_robin` balances every single RPC across all 24 pods immediately.
tradeOffs: Client-side `round_robin` eliminates single-client hot-spotting without proxy infrastructure.
Requires internal DNS visibility to pod IPs (not possible across public internet).
alternatives: AWS ALB (L7 gRPC target group) for external traffic.
failureModes: If `grpc.dns_min_time_between_resolutions_ms` is too high, newly scaled pods wait longer to receive traffic.

stages.learnerPrompt: At 1,000 client pods and 200 server pods, full-mesh `round_robin` creates 200,000 TCP sockets. How do you prevent connection table exhaustion?

referenceMaterial.summary: At 200,000 sockets, full-mesh client-side LB wastes memory (~50 KB/socket = 10 GB) and causes epoll/TLS churn. Migrate to gRPC-xDS subsetting or an L7 Envoy gateway tier.
approachSteps: Cap per-client subchannels using xDS subset load balancing (e.g., 16–24 endpoints per client).
Alternatively, route through a stateless Envoy L7 proxy tier of 20 pods (1,000×20 + 20×200 = 24,000 sockets).
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
# Envoy L7 upstream cluster with bounded connections
connect_timeout: 0.25s
type: STRICT_DNS
lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST
typed_extension_protocol_options:
  envoy.extensions.upstreams.http.v3.HttpProtocolOptions:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.upstreams.http.v3.HttpProtocolOptions
    explicit_http_config:
      http2_protocol_options:
        max_concurrent_streams: 250
tradeOffs: Envoy tier reduces total cluster sockets by 8x at the cost of ~0.4 ms p99 latency.
xDS subsetting keeps zero extra hops but requires running a control plane (Istio/Traffic Director).
alternatives: Topology-aware routing (same-AZ preference) to shrink cross-AZ connection meshes.
failureModes: Without subsetting, 1,000 clients × 200 servers exhausts conntrack tables and ephemeral ports.

stages.learnerPrompt: Even after enabling `round_robin`, 5% of RPCs fail with `UNAVAILABLE: io exception` during rolling deployments. What is missing?

referenceMaterial.summary: Kubernetes removes the pod from Endpoints asynchronously while sending SIGTERM. Without a `preStop` hook and `GOAWAY` grace period, the pod closes sockets before kube-proxy/CoreDNS updates propagate.
approachSteps: Add `lifecycle.preStop.exec` (`sleep 5`) so the pod stays alive while CoreDNS/EndpointSlices propagate.
Call `server.shutdown()` and `awaitTermination(20, SECONDS)` on SIGTERM to emit HTTP/2 GOAWAY.
tradeOffs: Adds 5 seconds to pod rollout time per pod.
Eliminates race-condition UNAVAILABLE errors during EndpointSlice propagation.
alternatives: Enable client-side gRPC `retryPolicy` for idempotent unary reads on `UNAVAILABLE`.
failureModes: Killing the process before `sleep 5` drops streams still in flight from clients with cached DNS.

spark.summary: HTTP/2 multiplexes thousands of gRPC calls over a single persistent TCP connection, causing L4 load balancers to pin all traffic from a client to one backend pod even after horizontal autoscaling.
spark.keyTakeaway: Solve HTTP/2 pinning by switching to client-side L7 round-robin over headless DNS, inserting an L7 Envoy proxy, or enforcing jittered server-side MAX_CONNECTION_AGE.

problem.title: Load Balancing gRPC & HTTP/2 Across Kubernetes Pods
problem.prompt: Your payment-ledger gRPC service runs on Kubernetes behind an AWS Network Load Balancer (L4). During a 10x traffic surge, HPA scales the backend from 4 to 24 pods, yet CPU stays at 98% on the original 4 pods while the 20 new pods sit at 3% CPU. Existing Java and Python gRPC clients keep sending 100% of their 45,000 RPS over their initial subchannels. Diagnose why L4 load balancing fails for HTTP/2 and design a zero-downtime fix.
requirements: Distribute gRPC RPCs evenly (<10% skew) across all 24 backend pods within 30 seconds of HPA scale-out.
Prevent connection storms or TLS handshake spikes when cycling long-lived HTTP/2 connections.
Support both Java (grpc-netty) and Python (grpcio) clients without dropping in-flight RPCs.
Maintain sub-15 ms p99 latency during pod scale-up and rolling deployments.
constraints: Peak aggregate throughput is 45,000 RPS across 120 client pods.
TLS 1.3 mTLS is mandatory on all service-to-service gRPC channels.
In-flight unary RPCs take up to 2 seconds and must complete gracefully before socket closure.

concept.whyItMatters: L4 load balancers (AWS NLB, kube-proxy iptables/IPVS) only inspect the TCP 4-tuple on SYN packets. Because HTTP/2 multiplexes all gRPC streams onto one long-lived TCP connection, L4 balancers never re-balance individual RPCs, turning autoscaling into a no-op for existing clients.
whenToUse: When deploying gRPC services on Kubernetes or behind L4 TCP load balancers with HPA autoscaling.
When client-to-server pod ratios are low (e.g., 10 clients to 20 servers), magnifying subchannel skew.
When rolling deployments replace backend pods and traffic must drain cleanly to new endpoints.
whenNotToUse: When clients already route through an L7 Envoy/Istio/Linkerd sidecar or gateway that balances per-request.
When using short-lived HTTP/1.1 connections without keep-alive (each request opens a new TCP socket).
keyPoints: gRPC ManagedChannel resolves DNS once at startup and opens one TCP connection per resolved IP.
Behind a ClusterIP or NLB VIP, DNS returns a single virtual IP, so each client opens exactly 1 TCP subchannel.
Server-side MAX_CONNECTION_AGE with jitter forces clients to re-resolve DNS and reconnect via GOAWAY.
Headless Kubernetes Services (clusterIP: None) combined with client-side round_robin enable true per-RPC balancing.
terms: Subchannel: A gRPC abstraction wrapping a single physical TCP/HTTP2 connection to a specific resolved backend endpoint.
HTTP/2 Multiplexing: Interleaving multiple concurrent RPC streams over a single TCP connection using 31-bit stream identifiers.
GOAWAY Frame: An HTTP/2 control frame instructing the peer to stop opening new streams on the connection while finishing active ones.

tradeOffs.factor: Client-Side LB (Headless DNS + round_robin) vs L7 Proxy (Envoy)
tradeOffs.pro: Client-side LB adds zero network hops (<0.2 ms overhead) and avoids operating a separate proxy tier.
tradeOffs.con: Requires every polyglot client (Java, Python, Go) to configure DNS polling and LB policies consistently.

tradeOffs.pro: 60s max age rebalances traffic onto newly scaled pods within a minute even behind an L4 VIP.
tradeOffs.con: Increases TLS 1.3 handshake CPU overhead and connection churn by 10x across all client pods.

failureModes.name: Synchronized Reconnection Stampede
failureModes.description: All backend pods enforce an identical 5-minute MAX_CONNECTION_AGE without jitter, causing 120 clients to tear down and re-handshake TLS simultaneously.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure MAX_CONNECTION_AGE_GRACE and +/- 15% random jitter on server connection age.

failureModes.name: Stale DNS Cache in JVM
failureModes.description: JVM caches headless service DNS records indefinitely or for 30s+, ignoring newly added Kubernetes pod IPs.
failureModes.mitigation: Use gRPC's built-in dns:/// NameResolver with periodic refresh or xDS control plane.

failureModes.name: Sticky L4 VIP Under Rolling Update
failureModes.description: Clients pinned to a single ClusterIP VIP never discover new pods until existing pods terminate.
failureModes.mitigation: Combine headless DNS with client-side round_robin or route through an L7 Envoy proxy.

commonMistakes: Increasing maxConcurrentStreams on the server thinking it will spread load across pods.
Deploying a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service with gRPC and expecting kube-proxy IPVS to balance individual RPCs.
Setting MAX_CONNECTION_AGE without MAX_CONNECTION_AGE_GRACE, abruptly aborting 2-second in-flight RPCs.
Leaving gRPC default loadBalancingPolicy as pick_first when using headless DNS, which still pins to IP #1.

sections.content:
## Why L4 Load Balancers Fail HTTP/2

In a traditional HTTP/1.1 architecture, clients open a pool of short-lived TCP connections, giving L4 load balancers (AWS NLB, `kube-proxy` iptables/IPVS) frequent TCP `SYN` packets to distribute across backend pods. gRPC uses **HTTP/2**, which opens **one persistent TCP connection** per resolved IP and multiplexes up to `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` (typically 100–1000) concurrent RPCs over that single socket.

When 120 client pods connect to `payment-ledger.prod.svc.cluster.local:9090` (a standard `ClusterIP` or NLB VIP), DNS returns **1 virtual IP**. Each client creates 1 subchannel. The L4 balancer hashes the 4-tuple on the initial `SYN` and pins that socket to one of the original 4 pods. When HPA adds 20 new pods, no new `SYN` packets arrive from existing clients—leaving the original 4 pods at **98% CPU** and the 20 new pods idle at **3% CPU**.

## Requirements & Constraints

* **Skew Tolerance**: RPC distribution across all 24 pods must stay within **<10% variance** within 30 seconds of HPA scale-out.
* **Zero Dropped RPCs**: In-flight unary calls lasting up to **2,000 ms** must finish before any connection closes.
* **mTLS Overhead**: With 120 client pods and 24 server pods, TLS 1.3 handshakes must be amortized so handshake CPU stays under **2% of total core budget**.
* **Polyglot Support**: Both Java (`grpc-netty-shaded`) and Python (`grpcio`) clients must work without custom C++ extensions.

## Capacity & Connection Math

* **Aggregate Traffic**: 45,000 RPS across 24 pods = **1,875 RPS/pod** (well below 10,000 RPS/pod ceiling).
* **With Headless DNS + `round_robin`**: 120 client pods × 24 server pods = **2,880 total TCP connections** cluster-wide (120 sockets per server pod, ~15.6 RPS per socket).
* **With Jittered `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` (180s ± 10%)**: 2,880 connections / 180s = **16 TLS 1.3 handshakes/sec** cluster-wide (<0.7 handshakes/sec per server pod), negligible CPU impact.

sections.content:
## Detailed Design

### 1. Headless Kubernetes Service + Client-Side `round_robin`
Expose the backend with `clusterIP: None` so CoreDNS returns all 24 pod IPs. Configure clients to use `round_robin` instead of the default `pick_first`.

### 2. Server-Side `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` with Grace & Jitter
Even with headless DNS, gRPC's Java `DnsNameResolver` only re-resolves when a subchannel fails or enters `IDLE`. Setting `maxConnectionAge` to **180 seconds** with **10% random jitter** and `maxConnectionAgeGrace` of **5 seconds** forces periodic HTTP/2 `GOAWAY` frames so clients discover new HPA pods automatically without dropping 2s in-flight calls.

### 3. Alternative: L7 Envoy Sidecar / Gateway
If clients cannot be reconfigured (e.g., third-party consumers behind an external NLB), place an Envoy L7 proxy in front of the backends. Envoy terminates client HTTP/2 streams and multiplexes individual requests across upstream pod endpoints via `ROUND_ROBIN` or `LEAST_REQUEST`.

## Failure Handling & Edge Cases

* **Pod Termination During `GOAWAY`**: Pair `maxConnectionAgeGrace(5, SECONDS)` with Kubernetes `preStop: sleep 5` and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` so pods stop accepting new streams before `SIGTERM`.
* **CoreDNS Cache TTL**: Ensure CoreDNS `cache` TTL for internal headless services is `<= 5s` so newly ready pods appear immediately.
* **Large Cluster Fan-Out**: Above ~200 client pods × 100 server pods (20,000 sockets), switch from full-mesh headless DNS to **xDS (gRPC-xDS / Istio)** with subsetting so each client only connects to a bounded subset of 15–20 pods.

## Production Resolution

1. Switch the Kubernetes Service to `clusterIP: None` (headless) and configure clients with `defaultLoadBalancingPolicy("round_robin")`.
2. Configure `NettyServerBuilder.maxConnectionAge(180, SECONDS)` (with ±10% jitter via `permitKeepAliveTime` / server config) and `maxConnectionAgeGrace(5, SECONDS)`.
3. Verify skew drops from **100%/0%** to **<5% variance** across all 24 pods in Prometheus (`grpc_server_started_total` per pod).
